title: Planting a dwarf apple
summary: In late winter while it is dormant, or from a pot until spring.
steps: Choose a dwarf rootstock and two kinds that bloom together, or one self-fertile kind.
In the ground, dig a hole twice as wide as the roots and no deeper, in full sun with good drainage. Keep the graft union 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in) above the soil.
In a pot, use at least 57 L (15 gal) and follow the basics guide for fruit trees in pots.
Water deeply, mulch, and stake dwarf trees; their roots are small.

title: Caring for and harvesting apples
summary: Prune in winter, thin in spring, pick in late summer and fall.
steps: Each winter, remove dead, crossing and upright shoots to keep the center open to light.
When fruits are marble sized, thin to one per cluster, about 15 cm (6 in) apart.
An apple is ripe when it lifts and twists off easily and the seeds are brown.
Store the best apples in a cold, humid place; turn bruised ones into sauce right away.

title: Planting a dwarf peach
summary: In late winter, in the sunniest spot you have.
steps: Pick a low-chill or high-chill kind to match your winters.
Plant with the graft union above the soil in well-drained ground, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot.
Avoid low spots where cold air settles on spring nights; the blossoms are tender.
Water deeply and mulch, keeping the mulch off the trunk.

title: Caring for and harvesting peaches
summary: Open the center, thin hard, pick when the green is gone.
steps: Prune in late winter to an open vase shape with three or four main branches.
Spray a copper or lime-sulfur dormant spray in late winter if leaf curl has been a problem, following the label.
Thin fruits to 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 in) apart when small.
Pick when the background color has no green and the fruit gives slightly. Rake up leaves and pruned twigs where goats can reach.

title: Planting a dwarf pear
summary: In late winter while dormant.
steps: Plant two kinds that bloom at the same time.
Plant in full sun with the graft union above the soil, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot.
Water deeply and mulch.

title: Caring for and harvesting pears
summary: Light pruning, early picking.
steps: Prune lightly in winter; heavy pruning encourages fire blight.
Cut out blackened, hooked shoot tips well below the damage, cleaning your pruners between cuts.
Pick European pears when they are full size and lift easily, then ripen them at room temperature for a few days.
To can pears, add lemon juice and follow a tested recipe; Asian pears are low enough in acid that the lemon juice is a must.

title: Planting a plum
summary: In late winter while dormant.
steps: Check whether your kind needs a partner, and plant two if it does.
Plant in full sun with the graft union above the soil, or a dwarf tree in a 57 L (15 gal) pot.
Water deeply and mulch.

title: Caring for and harvesting plums
summary: Thin the crop and keep cut branches from goats.
steps: Prune young trees in late winter to an open shape; older trees need only light thinning.
Thin fruits to 8 to 10 cm (3 to 4 in) apart so branches don't break.
Pick when the fruit is fully colored and slightly soft.
Gather pruned branches and fallen leaves right away where goats can reach them.

title: Planting an apricot
summary: In late winter, away from frost pockets.
steps: Choose a kind that blooms late or suits your chill hours.
Plant on higher ground or a slope where cold air drains away, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot you can move under cover.
Water deeply and mulch.

title: Caring for and harvesting apricots
summary: Protect the blossoms, then pick soft and sweet.
steps: Cover small trees with frost cloth on frosty nights while they bloom.
Prune lightly after harvest or in late winter.
Pick when the fruit is fully orange and gives slightly. Halve and dry extras on screens or in a dehydrator.
Keep pruned branches and fallen leaves away from goats.

title: Planting a persimmon
summary: In late winter while dormant.
steps: Persimmons have a long taproot; plant a young tree and don't disturb the roots.
Plant in full sun, or in a 76 L (20 gal) pot for a dwarf kind.
Water deeply and mulch. Young trees may drop fruit for a year or two; that is normal.

title: Caring for and harvesting persimmons
summary: Little pruning, a fall harvest.
steps: Prune only to remove dead or crossing branches.
Cut fruit with a bit of stem attached when it is fully orange.
Eat Fuyu types crisp; let Hachiya types soften on the counter until jelly-soft.

title: Planting a fig
summary: In spring around the last frost.
steps: Plant against a warm south or west wall in cooler places, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot.
Set it slightly deeper than it grew; figs root along buried stems.
Water deeply every week the first summer.

title: Caring for and harvesting figs
summary: Pick ripe, protect from hard frost.
steps: Prune in late winter only to shape and remove dead wood.
Pick figs when they droop and feel soft, wearing gloves against the sap.
Eat within a few days, dry them, or make preserves with lemon juice using a tested recipe.
Before hard freezes, move potted figs into an unheated garage or greenhouse, or wrap in-ground trees.

title: Planting a pomegranate
summary: In spring after the worst cold.
steps: Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot.
Water deeply until it is growing well, then water every week or two in summer.
Train it as a shrub with several stems or a small tree with one.

title: Caring for and harvesting pomegranates
summary: Steady water, fall harvest.
steps: Water evenly while fruit is growing; a sudden soaking after drought splits the fruit.
Remove suckers from the base and thin crowded branches in late winter.
Cut ripe fruit off with pruners when it is deeply colored and sounds metallic when tapped.

title: Planting a Meyer lemon in a pot
summary: In spring once frost is past.
steps: Choose a grafted tree and a 57 L (15 gal) pot with fast-draining citrus mix.
Keep the graft union well above the mix, and don't bury the trunk.
Water deeply, then let the top few centimeters dry before watering again.

title: Caring for and harvesting lemons
summary: Feed in summer, bring inside for frost.
steps: Feed with a citrus fertilizer from spring to late summer.
Move it inside to a bright, cool spot before nights fall to 0 °C (32 °F), and back out after the last frost, easing it into full sun over a week.
Pick lemons when fully yellow and slightly soft; they keep on the tree for weeks.

title: Planting a satsuma
summary: In spring after the last frost.
steps: In the ground, plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot with the graft union above the soil.
In colder places, grow it in a 57 L (15 gal) pot on wheels.
Water deeply and mulch, keeping the mulch off the trunk.

title: Caring for and harvesting satsumas
summary: Feed, protect, pick when sweet.
steps: Feed with citrus fertilizer in late winter, late spring and midsummer.
Cover young trees with frost cloth, or move pots under cover, before hard freezes.
Clip fruit off with a short stem when colored and sweet.

title: Planting an avocado
summary: In spring once nights are warm.
steps: Choose a grafted tree. Compact kinds suit a 76 L (20 gal) pot.
Plant in very well-drained soil, slightly raised in a mound if your soil is heavy. Never let it sit in water.
Plant it outside any area where goats or chickens roam.
Shade the trunk of a young tree with whitewash or a wrap against sunburn.

title: Caring for and harvesting avocados
summary: Deep water, thick mulch, pick and ripen indoors.
steps: Keep a thick layer of coarse mulch over the roots and water deeply but not often.
Protect from frost with cloth or move pots inside.
Pick a full-size fruit and let it soften on the counter for a week. If it ripens soft and tastes good, the rest are ready.

title: Planting a guava
summary: In warm weather.
steps: Plant in full sun, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot in colder places.
Water well and mulch.
Prune to a few main branches to keep it small.

title: Caring for and harvesting guavas
summary: Feed often, bag the fruit.
steps: Feed lightly every two months during the growing season.
Where fruit flies are common, slip small mesh bags over young fruit.
Pick when the skin turns yellowish and the fruit smells sweet; it softens in a day or two.

title: Planting blueberries
summary: In late winter or early spring.
steps: Test your soil. If it isn't acid (pH 4.5 to 5.5), grow them in pots of acid mix or in raised beds of peat and pine bark.
Plant two or more kinds of the same type, 1.5 m (5 ft) apart, at the same depth they grew.
Water with rainwater if your tap water is hard. Mulch with pine needles or bark.

title: Caring for and harvesting blueberries
summary: Net the berries, prune old canes.
steps: Feed with a fertilizer for acid-loving plants in spring.
Net the bushes when berries start to color.
Pick berries a few days after they turn fully blue; they come off with a gentle roll of the thumb.
After the third year, cut out one or two of the oldest canes each winter.

title: Planting thornless blackberries
summary: In late winter or early spring.
steps: Put up a trellis first: two wires at about 0.9 and 1.5 m (3 and 5 ft) high.
Plant 90 cm (3 ft) apart along it, or one per 57 L (15 gal) pot with a cage.
Water deeply and mulch.

title: Caring for and harvesting blackberries
summary: Tie new canes, cut old ones.
steps: Tie new canes to the trellis as they grow.
Pick when berries turn dull black and come off easily, every two or three days.
After harvest, cut the canes that fruited to the ground.

title: Planting raspberries
summary: In late winter or early spring.
steps: Choose fall-bearing kinds for the simplest care, and a spot with afternoon shade in hot places.
Plant 60 cm (2 ft) apart in rows or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot.
Cut canes to 15 cm (6 in) after planting and keep them mulched and moist.

title: Caring for and harvesting raspberries
summary: Pick often, mow in winter.
steps: Pick every day or two at peak, when berries pull off easily.
For fall-bearing kinds, cut all canes to the ground in late winter.
Pull suckers that wander out of the row.

title: Planting elderberries
summary: In late winter or early spring.
steps: Plant two kinds 1.8 m (6 ft) apart in sun or part shade; damp ground is fine.
Plant outside pastures and pens where goats or other livestock could reach the leaves.
Water well the first year and mulch.

title: Caring for and harvesting elderberries
summary: Cut whole clusters, always cook.
steps: Cut whole clusters when nearly all berries are dark.
Freeze clusters, then rub the berries off; discard stems and green berries.
Cook berries before eating, in jam, pie or jelly.
Each winter, cut out canes older than three years.

title: Planting strawberries
summary: In early spring, or in fall where winters are mild.
steps: Plant in full sun, 30 cm (12 in) apart, in rich soil or an 11 L (3 gal) pot for a few plants.
Set the crown exactly at soil level: buried crowns rot and exposed roots dry out.
Mulch with straw and water evenly.

title: Caring for and harvesting strawberries
summary: Pick every other day, renew every few years.
steps: Pinch off the first flowers on June-bearing plants the first spring so the plants grow strong.
Pick berries when fully red, with the cap on, in the cool of the morning.
Root a few runners each summer into small pots to replace old plants.

title: Planting a pineapple guava
summary: In spring.
steps: Plant in full sun or light shade, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot.
Plant two if your kind needs a partner.
Water well until settled; after that it handles dry spells.

title: Caring for and harvesting feijoas
summary: Little care; gather fallen fruit.
steps: Prune lightly after harvest to shape.
Gather fruit as it drops, every day, and let it soften for a day or two.
Scoop out the pulp with a spoon. Pick a few petals from the flowers for salads.

title: Planting goji
summary: In late winter or early spring.
steps: Plant in full sun, 1.2 m (4 ft) apart, or in a 38 L (10 gal) pot.
It tolerates poor and alkaline soil but needs good drainage.
Give it a fence or trellis to lean on.

title: Caring for and harvesting goji
summary: Prune hard, pick red and soft.
steps: In late winter, prune to a few main stems and shorten side shoots.
Pull suckers that come up away from the plant.
Pick berries fully red and soft, and dry them on screens.

title: Planting a grapevine
summary: In late winter or early spring.
steps: Put up an arbor, fence or two-wire trellis first.
Plant 2.4 m (8 ft) apart, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot with a sturdy frame.
After planting, cut the vine back to two or three buds and let one strong shoot grow up the support.

title: Caring for and harvesting grapes
summary: Prune hard every winter, taste for ripeness.
steps: Each winter, remove most of last year's growth, leaving short spurs of two buds along the main arms.
Thin leaves around clusters in summer for air and sun.
Cut clusters when the grapes taste sweet; they don't sweeten after picking.

title: Planting muscadines
summary: In late winter or early spring.
steps: Put up a single wire about 1.5 m (5 ft) high, or an arbor.
Plant 5 m (16 ft) apart, with at least one self-fertile kind for every few female ones.
Water deeply and mulch.

title: Caring for and harvesting muscadines
summary: Shorten the shoots in winter, pick over weeks.
steps: Each winter, cut the shoots along the arms back to short spurs of two or three buds.
Gather ripe grapes as they drop, or spread a sheet and shake the vine.
Make jelly or juice from extras.

title: Planting passion fruit
summary: Once frost is past and nights are warm.
steps: Plant against a strong fence or trellis in full sun, or in a 57 L (15 gal) pot with a frame.
Water deeply and mulch.
Move pots under cover before frost.

title: Caring for and harvesting passion fruit
summary: Thin the vine, gather fallen fruit.
steps: Thin tangled growth after harvest.
Feed lightly every month in summer.
Gather fruit that drops; it is sweetest after it wrinkles a little.

title: Planting hardy kiwi
summary: In early spring.
steps: Build a strong arbor or T-bar trellis first; the vine gets heavy.
Plant one male for every several females, 4.5 m (15 ft) apart, unless your kind is self-fertile.
Protect new shoots from late frost with cloth.

title: Caring for and harvesting hardy kiwi
summary: Prune twice a year, pick firm.
steps: Prune in winter to a framework of arms, and trim long shoots in summer.
Pick firm fruit when the seeds inside have turned black.
Soften the fruit at room temperature for a few days, then eat skin and all.

title: Planting chayote
summary: After the last frost, from a sprouting fruit.
steps: Buy a firm chayote and leave it on the counter until a shoot appears from the wide end.
Plant the whole fruit on its side with the shoot end slightly up, half buried, next to a strong trellis.
Water well and mulch thickly.

title: Caring for and harvesting chayote
summary: Lots of growth, a fall harvest.
steps: Keep it watered through summer; the vine can grow many meters.
Pick fruits when they are 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 in) long and still tender.
Where winters are mild, cut the vine down after frost and mulch the root heavily.

title: Planting dragon fruit
summary: In warm weather.
steps: Set a sturdy post 1.5 to 1.8 m (5 to 6 ft) tall, with a frame or old tire on top for the stems to drape over.
Plant three rooted cuttings around the post, or one in a 57 L (15 gal) pot with its own post, in fast-draining cactus mix.
Tie the stems to the post as they grow, and water only when the mix is dry.

title: Caring for and harvesting dragon fruit
summary: Hand-pollinate at night, pick colored fruit.
steps: When a flower opens at night, brush pollen from its center onto the same or another flower if your kind needs it.
Pick the fruit about a month later, when it is fully colored and gives slightly.
Move pots inside before nights drop near 4 °C (40 °F).
